title: Kett and the Glittering Crows
markdown:
High above the bustling valleys, where waterfalls cascaded like silver ribbons and orchards bloomed with fruit that tasted of starlight, lived the mountain goblins. Their homes, carved into rock, were marvels of ingenious building. Among them lived Kett, fingers as nimble as his mind, pockets jingling with polished pebbles, iridescent beetle wings, bits of discarded metal. He wasn’t mean. He did have a knack for what other goblins affectionately, and sometimes with a sigh, called shiny mistakes: happy accidents of invention, a hastily fashioned contraption gleaming just so, debris catching light unexpectedly.

His dearest friend was Rivulet, a ferret of sleek fur and boundless energy, eyes sparkling with almost human intelligence. Not merely a pet: confidante, shadow, often the quiet wisdom Kett overlooked in bursts of creation. A wet-nose nudge, a specific chitter Kett understood as clearly as speech. Their bond was granite.

One sun-drenched morning the annual Mountain Blossom Festival pulsed: laughter, hollowed-reed music, honeyed pastries. Kett found himself near the grandest stall, where the renowned mountaineer Glint Pebblefoot displayed her trophies. Weathered face, eyes that held sky and mountain resolve. Kett clutched a shard of quartz polished until it gleamed like a captured star.

“A fine piece, young goblin,” Glint boomed, surprisingly gentle, distant thunder with warmth. “But have you ever felt the wind bite at Serpent’s Tooth? That is a challenge worthy of true courage. The air there sings with a song only the bravest can hear.”

A spark. “Serpent’s Tooth. I’ve imagined its slopes a thousand times. I know its every twist and turn.”

Glint chuckled, stones tumbling a gentle slope. “Your spirit is as bright as that quartz. A friendly contest, then. You and I. A race to the summit. My usual route, yours as you see fit.”

The next dawn, first blush of rose and gold on snow-caps, Kett and Rivulet stood at the base. The mountain loomed, ancient beast of rock and ice. Pack of tools, coil of sturdy vine, snacks of roasted nuts and sweet berries. Toes tingling. Rivulet on his shoulder mapped pine, damp earth, crisp high air.

They had barely begun through orchards heavy with ruby-red apples, skins cool and firm, when they paused. The trees held the morning. Blossom-scent from the festival still clung to Kett’s tunic. Rivulet sniffed a fallen apple as if it were a map. For a few breaths the race did not matter; only the orchard did, and the way light sat on fruit that tasted, the stories said, of starlight.

Then a shimmer moved in the sky: whisper of wings, silk in a breeze. Snow-crows descended, feathers catching nascent light like polished obsidian. Intelligent jet eyes fixed not on Kett but on small glittering objects tumbling from his pouch as he scrambled — a loose button, a dropped nut, a misplaced pebble that winked.

“Shiny mistakes,” Kett muttered, pulling the pouch closer. “They like the shiny mistakes.” Not aggressive. Interested. Calls like tiny delicate bells, musical and slightly unsettling.

He tried shooing, arms waving with comical urgency. Rivulet shifted nervously. The crows found his efforts amusing, swooped closer. Rivulet chittered a low warning: they are not afraid. They are intrigued.

“They’re following us. And Glint will be far ahead if this carries on.” He tied string to a shiny metal spool and swung it. The crows darted and weaved, aerial acrobatics, until he retrieved it with a sigh.

A peculiar procession. A makeshift grappling hook of vine and bent picnic-spoon might slip; the spoon might clatter; presto, another shiny mistake. A constant glittering distraction, a playful feathery escort.

Near the ice-fields the wind grew colder, biting. A sheer wall of ice, glazed and slippery, mirrored the stark sky. He was contemplating a risky maneuver when agitated squawks burst above. The crows, eager to snatch a loose icicle that glittered like diamond, had gathered in a dense swirl over the most precarious section. Combined weight dislodged a larger slab. It tumbled perilously close with a roar.

Kett ducked, heart pounding. They weren’t trying to harm him. They were attracted to the sparkle of a mistake. And in their eager pursuit they could make their own rather significant accidental ones.

He looked at Rivulet, idea alight, and rummaged not for tools but for a small intricately carved whistle of polished bone, smooth and cool. Clear resonant notes. He blew.

The crows paused, heads tilted. He began to ascend not by brute force but with careful deliberate movements. With each handhold a tiny shard of ice tumbled, catching light with a brief inviting sparkle. Not mistakes: small controlled flashes of brilliance.

He whistled again, softer, a gentle beckoning. The crows, drawn by the cascade of tiny glittering fragments, followed the smaller pieces. Their descent from the main icefall made a safe, albeit shimmering, path. Guided by their own fascination. Rivulet gave a tiny approving chirp.

With the crows busy in their scavenger hunt, bell-calls a cheerful accompaniment, Kett and Rivulet reached the summit of Serpent’s Tooth just as Glint arrived. She greeted him with a hearty laugh. “Well done. I saw those feathered fiends causing a stir. You handled them with more grace than I might have. A clever solution, to turn their fascination into a pathway.”

They had not vanquished the snow-crows. They had understood them. Glint clasped his shoulder, strong and firm.

They stood a moment in the thin bright air, apples still a rumour far below, crows stitching the sky with leftover gleam. Glint offered him a strip of dried fruit from her own pack; he offered her a pebble that had survived the pouch. Neither called it a prize.

Then they started down together, not as rivals so much as two climbers who had heard the same mountain song and answered it differently. Home would still jingle with pebbles and beetle wings. Rivulet would still nudge when invention ran ahead of sense. The shiny mistakes would still happen. Some of them, if you whistled kindly, might even show you the way up.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
